newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Zaireans gather for food distribution in Goma.
newsitem.headline: Zaireans gather for food distribution in Goma.

text.p: Aid workers returned to rebel-held Goma in eastern Zaire on Tuesday for a second attempt to distribute food while Canada was said to have volunteered to lead a multinational force to end the refugee crisis.
The aid workers entered from Rwanda despite Zaire saying they were violating its sovereignty.
With rebel supporters wielding sticks to keep them under control, some 2,500 Zaireans crowded around a U.N. warehouse in Goma city, waiting for a distribution of aid agency biscuits.
Officials said food and medical supplies brought into Zaire from Rwanda on Tuesday would be distributed to three hospitals in Goma.
A symbolic amount of food, medical supplies and blankets trucked into Goma by U.N. and independent aid agencies on Monday was the first aid to reach eastern Zaire from Rwanda since April last year.
It was kept overnight at a football stadium under rebel guard in largely-looted Goma, which has some 200,000 people.

Canada offered on Monday to lead a multinational force to help end the crisis in eastern Zaire and bring vital relief to more than a million Hutu refugees displaced by four weeks' of fighting, U.N. sources said in New York.
Canadian ambassador Robert Fowler offered the troops at an informal meeting at the United Nations, thereby making the likelihood of a force more probable, the senior sources added.
The main motor behind the force idea, France, is rejected as partial by the Tutsi military in Rwanda and by the Zairean rebels who have captured the east's main towns.

There was speculation in the region on Tuesday that two foreign interventions might be in gestation -- a civilian effort from Rwanda into rebel areas and a Canadian-commanded military one from government-held parts of Zaire.
Most of the 1.2 million Hutu refugees from Rwanda and Burundi are sandwiched between these two areas.
In Kinshasa, Zairean Information Minister Boguo Makele told Reuters Zaire had no objection to aid arriving in the country via the capital and being distributed to displaced Zaireans.
But he denounced aid taken into Goma from Rwanda. "This constitutes a violation of our territorial integrity," he said. "Aid for the (Rwanda) refugees should be distributed in Rwanda."
"The decision to send in aid was taken by the (U.N.) secretary-general based on the fact there is a humanitarian crisis," said U.N. World Food Programme spokeswoman Michelle Quintaglie on Tuesday.
"With a humanitarian crisis as big as this we have no other option but to go in and make sure people receive assistance."
"There is massive human suffering," said a spokeswoman for Medecins sans Frontieres (Doctors Without Frontiers), taking in more supplies on Tuesday. "We will do whatever we have to do."
The world has watched and waited as the crisis unfolds. A Franco-Spanish intervention plan hit road-blocks but the same force led by Canada would be seen as more neutral, diplomats say.
"We will need other contributors, notably the United States," said a senior diplomat at the U.N. adding he believed the Canadians would also want Washington's participation.
More than a million Hutus fled from Rwanda to Zaire in fear of reprisals in 1994 after Hutu hardliners massacred hundreds of thousands of minority Tutsis and their sympathisers.
South African President Nelson Mandela changed tack on Monday and said he was also prepared to send troops to central Africa. But he wanted more specific information first, he said.
The United States denied it was blocking the creation of an international force but said it had still not seen a coherent plan for assembling one.
U.S. State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns, speaking to reporters accompanying Secretary of State Warren Christopher to a conference in Cairo, said Washington recognised a force was needed.
"The United States is not trying to block that force," he said. "We are trying to help that force take shape."

The other major Western powers with the means have reacted coolly to the proposal. The U.N. Security Council called on Friday for such a force but set no date for it, to the anger of international humanitarian organisations.

The Tutsi-led government in Rwanda, which supports the rebellion in Zaire, opposes the use of French troops. It accuses France of sympathy for armed Hutus in the refugee camps who led the 1994 genocide and then fled into Zaire with Hutu civilians.
